headline: Lauren Cassidy finds relief in improving US consumer credit metrics and a cooler-than-expected June CPI print
reasoning: The US consumer had been the primary area of concern, but Cassidy was relieved to see credit card delinquencies and net charge-offs improve across money-centre banks, continuing a trend from May monthly data. The June CPI came in at 3.5% versus an expectation of 3.8%, driven by lower oil prices, though oil has since ticked up in July. Cassidy notes this avoided a potential double-whammy of bad news and prevented a negative market reaction, but says the consumer still warrants close monitoring.
quote: So we saw a consumer credit within the credit cards improved. So both late and missed payments delinquencies and net charge offs improved. We saw that as a continuation from the May monthly data. And then to my relief, we also had the consumer price index or our measure of inflation come down. And so that was 3.5% 3.8 was expected. So a little bit cooler for the month reading of June mostly because oil prices came down in June. Now they have ticked up a little bit in July. So we'll have to keep a close eye on the consumer.
episode_title: Where the contrarian value lies among US banks

headline: Lauren Cassidy takes a contrarian buy on Citigroup, arguing the market is underestimating CEO Jane Fraser's turnaround
reasoning: Citigroup disappointed the market by leaving full-year guidance unchanged, implying a softer back half, but Cassidy disagrees with that read. She believes the multi-decade restructuring effort is working, and that Citi's partnership with Palantir — first deployed in wealth management — is delivering greater real-time visibility and sharper decision-making across the company. The guidance caution was viewed by Cassidy as prudence rather than a warning sign, making the post-results dip a buying opportunity. She argues the market is underestimating both the CEO and the bank.
quote: I actually really I think it's a buy on the dip story here. I think that, um, they've been working with Palantir and they used it their technology in wealth management first, and they're continuing to have greater visibility and real time information. They can make sharper decisions across the company with. So I think this restructuring works. They've been trying to restructure this business for decades. So I think city is a wonderful buy here.

headline: Lauren Cassidy describes choppy US jobs data as reflecting an AI-driven transition, with average tech and financial job losses of 28,000 per month year-to-date
reasoning: Cassidy acknowledges the non-farm payroll data has been choppy and that the Fed faces a difficult task. She estimates average losses of around 28,000 jobs per month across technology and financials year-to-date, which she attributes most likely to AI adoption. Drawing on six historical technology waves, she argues the transition will ultimately result in greater prosperity and job creation, though a transition period of disruption is expected.
quote: The debate continues on. You know, how many jobs are we going to lose through this transition? If you look back through American history, there's been six major waves. So we had the steam engine, electricity, modern manufacturing led by Ford computers, the internet. And now we have AI. And while we came out the other end with greater prosperity and job creation on, um, through all of those waves, there was always a transition period. And we're seeing that now. So, um, you know, we've had average losses of about 28,000 jobs a month across technology and financials, and that's most likely due to AI year to date.

headline: Lauren Cassidy notes AI-adopting companies are growing workforces while non-adopters are losing jobs, with entry-level roles up 12%
reasoning: Cassidy references a study from Ramp and Rebellion Labs showing that companies spending at least $30 per month per employee on AI added 10% to their workforce over two years, led by 12% gains in entry-level jobs. She argues the job losses in the broader economy reflect workers not using AI losing out to those who are. This frames the AI transition as a productivity and workforce reshaping story rather than a net job destruction story.
quote: There was a study this week that came out from Ramp and Rebellion Labs, and it showed that top spenders of AI, where a company is spending at least $30 a month per employee, actually over the next two years, ended up adding 10% to its workforce, which a lot of people, um, you know, previously didn't expect. And that's actually led by 12% gains for entry level jobs. So those companies are taking advantage of AI. So I think we're we're losing jobs in the economy is, uh, people working without AI are losing to people who are working with AI.
